segment_name: Opening: A Town of Peculiar Habits

questions.question: Oliver, you've said these passages are basically scored like music — that the rhythm of the prose is the joke. Can you actually demonstrate that? Take the poker expedition — what does it sound like when you read it aloud, and why does the rhythm matter?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to read the poker passage aloud and make a concrete case for the performance-art argument, setting up a contrast with Daniel's darker reading of the same scene

questions.question: Daniel, Oliver's hearing comedy and bravura in that poker scene — you're hearing something quite different. You said those women have been turned into unpaid guardians of property, armed with kitchen implements. That's a pretty bleak way to read what looks like a fun scene. Make the case.
questions.intent: Force Daniel to articulate his class-critique reading against the grain of what sounds like a charming passage — provoke Edmund to defend the women's genuine courage

questions.question: Edmund, you said the domestic sphere here isn't a prison metaphor — it's where virtue actually gets tested. But Daniel's just argued the whole system is designed to make these women police themselves on behalf of property. Can both of those things be true at once, or does one reading kill the other?
questions.intent: Force a direct confrontation between Edmund's moral-agency reading and Daniel's structural-critique — this is the central disagreement and needs to be explicit

questions.question: Here's the thing that bothers me about your reading, Daniel — Gaskell clearly loves these women. She's not holding them up for exposure. So is she oblivious to what you're describing, or is she doing something more complicated than critique?
questions.intent: Push Daniel on authorial sympathy versus structural analysis — does Gaskell endorse the system or mourn it? This should draw Edmund and Oliver in to defend Gaskell's intentions

questions.question: Edmund, all three of you want to quote the same line — 'Oh, gentility! can you endure this last shock?' But you're reading it completely differently. Oliver hears punctuation as performance, Daniel hears a trapped narrator recognising a system, you hear compassion under pressure. Same seven words. Who's right?
questions.intent: Use the shared passage to crystallise the three-way interpretive disagreement in a concrete, almost playful way — good radio moment, lets all three stake a position in quick succession

steering_notes: The productive tension here is between Oliver's formalist-performance reading, Daniel's materialist-critique reading, and Edmund's moral-realist reading — they're not just disagreeing about tone, they're disagreeing about what the novel is fundamentally for. Keep pressing on specific passages rather than general claims; the moment things go abstract, bring it back to the text. The poker scene and the 'Oh gentility' line are the live wires. Don't let Edmund and Daniel's disagreement become a seminar — frame it as a genuine argument about whether these women are agents or victims, and let Oliver's musicality angle cut through when the debate gets too heavy.
cross_engagement_targets: Oliver reads the poker passage aloud as performance — Daniel should immediately reframe the same passage as tragedy, not comedy; let that clash land before moving on
Edmund says the domestic implements represent real moral courage — Daniel's 'unpaid guardians of property' line is a direct contradiction; name that explicitly and ask them to resolve it
All three share the 'Oh gentility' quote but interpret it differently — this is the moment to ask them to sit in the same seven words and disagree out loud
Daniel's question 'who are the robbers?' has no answer in any of the other pre-interviews — it's worth flagging as a silence that neither Oliver nor Edmund has addressed

segment_name: The Genteel Trap: Miss Matty's Slow Unravelling

questions.question: Oliver, you said in our chat that c12:p35 is where the whole tragedy lives — that moment where Miss Matty 'hastily checks herself up.' Can you just read that bit and tell us what you're actually hearing in the rhythm of that sentence? Because I want to understand: is she lying to herself, or does she genuinely not know what she's doing?
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to perform the passage and open up the question of self-knowledge versus self-deception — sets up the Leigh/Rosen disagreement immediately

questions.question: Daniel, you called the line 'God ordains it all, and I am very happy' the most dangerous sentence in the passage — which is a provocative thing to say about what sounds like simple contentment. Edmund, I suspect, thinks that's exactly the point: that it's *not* dangerous, it's earned. So Dan, make the case: why is that sentence an alarm bell rather than a resolution?
questions.intent: Provoke the core Leigh-Rosen disagreement about whether Miss Matty's resignation is moral dignity or ideological capitulation — force Rosen to be specific about what he means by 'dangerous'

questions.question: Edmund, you're shaking your head — I can see it. You've said Gaskell is showing us moral necessity, not social pathology. But here's what I want to push on: Rosen's reading and yours actually both agree that Miss Matty has internalized deprivation. You just disagree about whether that's tragic or admirable. So which is it — and can it be both?
questions.intent: Force Leigh to either concede the tragic dimension or double down, and open up the question of whether the novel is asking us to admire Miss Matty or mourn her

questions.question: Let's go back to Miss Pole for a second — c12:p33, her little speech about spinsters being wiser than married women. Oliver, you called it Gaskell being 'comic and cruel at once.' But is Miss Pole the joke, or is she the warning? Because there's a version of this where Miss Pole is actually telling the truth and just telling it badly.
questions.intent: Use Miss Pole as a wedge to get at the feminist reading versus the tragic reading — Trevelyan's theatrical instincts should produce something vivid, and it gives Rosen a chance to make the ideological argument

questions.question: Daniel, final question for this section — and I want all three of you on this. You've said Miss Matty's contentment at the end is 'the most successful operation of the class and gender system in the entire novel.' But here's the uncomfortable thing: it also genuinely moves us. Does the fact that it works emotionally make Gaskell complicit in the system she's exposing? Or is that exactly the point?
questions.intent: Close the segment on the novel's deepest ambiguity — is Gaskell critiquing the system or aestheticizing it? Forces all three experts to take a final position

steering_notes: The productive tension in this segment is between Leigh's moral-theological reading and Rosen's ideological one, with Trevelyan as the literary-craft swing vote who can see both. Don't let the Leigh-Rosen debate become abstract — keep pulling them back to specific words in the passages. The phrase 'hastily checking herself up' and the 'God ordains it all' line should be quoted aloud at least once each. Watch for Trevelyan's instinct to aestheticize the tragedy — it's his strongest mode but can let the political argument slide. The goal is to end the segment with the question genuinely unresolved: is Miss Matty's happiness real, and does it matter if it was manufactured for her?
cross_engagement_targets: Leigh and Rosen both quote c12:p38 but read it as moral triumph vs. ideological surrender — make them address each other's reading directly rather than talking past it
Trevelyan's claim that 'the con works because everyone wants it to work' is more generous than Rosen's reading but more tragic than Leigh's — push him to locate himself between them
Rosen's 'sour-grapeism' argument and Leigh's 'moral necessity' argument are actually about the same psychological mechanism — get them to agree on the mechanism before they fight about its value

Trevelyan's theatrical reading of Miss Matty's hesitation ('it's in the rhythm') is a potential bridge between Leigh's interiority focus and Rosen's structural critique — use it to stop the debate becoming binary

segment_name: The Captain's Fall: Class and Consequence

questions.question: Daniel, you want to quote Miss Brown saying she 'did so little to cheer him'—and you read that as the system's perfect product, a woman blaming herself for not sacrificing enough. But isn't Gaskell inviting us to feel the pathos there, not the indictment? Walk me through why you think she's diagnosing rather than mourning.
questions.intent: Get Rosen to lay out his structural entrapment argument in full, and set up Leigh's counter that this is a moral rather than economic tragedy

questions.question: Edmund, I suspect you heard Daniel just now and wanted to throw something. You've said the obstacle here isn't class—it's filial love, full stop. But doesn't that reading let Major Gordon off the hook a bit? He leaves in a huff, travels the East, and comes back when it's convenient. Is that really just a failure of moral imagination, or is something colder going on?
questions.intent: Get Leigh to defend his moral reading while also prodding him on Gordon's culpability—he was sharp about Gordon in pre-interview and should be pushed to say it plainly

questions.question: Oliver, you've called the Major Gordon subplot a comic set-piece—a man learning about his beloved's father's death from a newspaper in Rome. That's a genuinely strange thing to say about what feels like a sad chapter. Make the case. What is Gaskell actually doing with that image, and why does it matter that it's almost farcical?
questions.intent: Draw out Trevelyan's 'forms of knowledge' argument and his reading of Galignani passage c3:p98—get him to read it aloud if possible

questions.question: Edmund, Oliver just read that passage—the matter-of-fact tone of Gordon learning about death from a foreign newspaper. Does that land for you as comedy, or does Gaskell's prose feel like something else entirely? Because you and Oliver seem to be describing the same words very differently.
questions.intent: Create direct cross-engagement between Leigh and Trevelyan on the question of Gaskell's register—is it tragic, comic, or both—and force Leigh to either concede the irony or push back hard

questions.question: Daniel, final push from me: Edmund says the tragedy would be equally tragic in a drawing-room of equals—class is beside the point. Oliver says it's really about who knows what and when. You're saying it's about structural entrapment. Can all three of those be true at once, or does one of them have to give way?
questions.intent: Force a synthesis moment that lets all three experts clarify where they genuinely disagree rather than talking past each other—should produce either a productive concession or a clean argument

steering_notes: This segment has the potential to get abstract fast—keep pulling back to the specific passages. Rosen and Leigh are the sharpest disagreement: one reads exploitation dressed as virtue, the other reads moral failure dressed as social critique. Trevelyan is the wild card who can either mediate or detonate depending on whether his comedy reading gets taken seriously. Let Leigh and Rosen go at each other on Gordon's return—Leigh thinks it's opportunistic, Rosen thinks it's a cold class calculation, and Trevelyan thinks it's almost slapstick. That three-way is the best radio in this segment. Don't let anyone stay too long in abstraction—the passages at c3:p76, c3:p97, and c3:p98 are vivid enough that reading aloud should be encouraged.
cross_engagement_targets: Rosen's reading of Miss Brown's guilt as 'manufactured' directly contradicts Leigh's claim that it is the moral heart of the passage—force them to argue about the same quote
Leigh dismisses the social programme reading but his own critique of Gordon (petulance, self-regard) actually supports Rosen's structural argument—point this out and see if either notices

Trevelyan's 'forms of knowledge' framing potentially reconciles Rosen and Leigh if they'd let it: Rosen says the system is invisible to victims, Leigh says characters fail to imagine each other's needs, Trevelyan says the gap between interior truth and external fact is where tragedy lives—these are compatible and worth surfacing

Leigh and Trevelyan both want to quote c3:p97 but for completely different reasons—Leigh for the moral contrast, Trevelyan for the comedy of misunderstanding—let them both read it and then ask the room which Gaskell intended

segment_name: Narrative Sleight of Hand: How Gaskell Tells Her Story

questions.question: Oliver, you said something in our chat that stuck with me — that this novel is basically 'written for the audiobook.' You want to take us to that moment where Miss Jessie's voice quivers and then steadies, passage c3:p77, and explain what you mean by Gaskell planting the microphone in exactly the right place?
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to perform or at least vividly describe the passage, establishing the 'trained ear' thesis early — and set up Edmund to agree for completely different reasons, and Daniel to immediately complicate both

questions.question: Daniel, you heard what Oliver just said — that the quivering voice is about intimacy, Gaskell pulling us close. You've called that same passage a kind of distraction. So I want to ask you directly: are you saying Gaskell is doing something dishonest here, or is it more complicated than that?
questions.intent: Force Rosen to sharpen his critique without letting him off the hook with academic hedging — the word 'dishonest' should provoke both Leigh and Trevelyan

questions.question: Edmund, you came in pretty fired up about Mrs Fitz-Adam — you called her love 'charity in its truest sense' — and you want to quote that line, 'I have loved her ever since, though perhaps I'd no right to do it.' But Daniel is sitting here saying that sentence contains the entire logic of a system that forces generosity underground. Who's right about what Gaskell is actually doing with that passage?
questions.intent: Create a direct three-way collision on c15:p104 — Leigh reads spiritual grace, Rosen reads structural coercion, Trevelyan has a third angle about love preceding judgment — let all three fight it out

questions.question: Let's go to the Miss Barker scene, c8:p21 — 'I must draw a line somewhere.' Oliver, you said she's terrified, not a snob. Daniel, you said the novel lets characters do the dirty work of exclusion while the narrator keeps her hands clean. Can you two actually sort out whether Gaskell is critiquing that line-drawing or just... fondly observing it?
questions.intent: Direct Trevelyan-Rosen confrontation on the question of whether comedy and critique can coexist — is sympathy the same as complicity?

questions.question: Edmund, I want to end on something you said that I can't quite let go: that Gaskell 'trusts us to feel without being told.' But Daniel's whole argument is that the feeling is the trick — we feel so much we stop asking questions. Is there a version of Cranford where both of you are right at the same time?
questions.intent: Push Leigh to either defend or qualify his 'moral education' thesis in direct response to Rosen's ideological critique — aiming for a genuinely unresolved ending that doesn't tidy the disagreement away

steering_notes: The big fault line is Leigh vs Rosen — spiritual sincerity versus ideological mystification — with Trevelyan as the most mobile voice, able to side with either depending on the passage. Don't let Trevelyan become a referee; push him to commit. The Queen Adelaide caps passage (c8:p5) is available as a comic release valve if the conversation gets too heavy. Rosen is the most likely to go abstract; pull him back to specific sentences. Leigh is the most likely to get eloquent but evasive; the word 'trick' or 'dishonest' tends to sharpen him. The goal is not resolution — the segment should end with the question genuinely open.
cross_engagement_targets: Trevelyan's 'intimacy' reading of c3:p77 directly contradicts Rosen's 'distraction' reading of the same passage — this is the sharpest collision and should be established early

Leigh and Rosen both want to quote the Mrs Fitz-Adam line ('I have loved her ever since, though perhaps I'd no right to do it') but read it as near-opposites: grace vs. structural coercion — make them quote it against each other
Trevelyan's claim that 'love precedes judgment' in the Fitz-Adam arc is a third position that neither Leigh nor Rosen has fully addressed — use it to stop the Leigh-Rosen binary from dominating

Rosen's point that emotional sincerity is mistaken for moral clarity is a direct challenge to Leigh's 'moral education' thesis — if Leigh doesn't respond to it unprompted, the final question should force the confrontation

segment_name: The Ghost in the Machine: Peter's Absence and Return

questions.question: Oliver, you've called Peter's letter in chapter seven the 'technical heart' of this whole segment — that moment where he says 'I must see you again before that time.' Can you read us that passage and tell us why Gaskell gives us Peter's voice *there*, in that one raw burst, and nowhere else? What's she doing structurally by making him so vivid precisely when he's about to disappear?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to perform the passage and articulate his 'ghost in the space' reading — sets up the central tension between Oliver's structural/performative take and the others' more thematic readings

questions.question: Edmund, you read that same letter as the whole moral drama in miniature — duty against love, pride against need. But Daniel, I suspect, wants to say something rather different about why Peter ends up at sea at all. Edmund, when the father puts that shawl in the grave and says 'Peter shall have that comfort' — is that the father *loving* his son, or is it the father managing his own guilt? Because those feel like very different things.
questions.intent: Force Edmund to defend his 'moral imagination' reading against the implicit class-guilt interpretation Daniel will press — gets the burial shawl passage in play early and creates real friction

questions.question: Daniel, I want to push on that word 'comfortable' — you flagged it from the Lady Glenmire passage, chapter nine: 'it was also very comfortable to find... that she was far removed from the vulgarity of wealth.' You called it the exact language of class anxiety, a constant audit. But Oliver thinks Gaskell is actually *delighted* by these women catching themselves being narrow-minded and adjusting. Who's right? Is Gaskell inside the joke with her characters, or is she watching them from a safe, diagnostic distance?
questions.intent: Directly engineer the Oliver-versus-Daniel disagreement about Gaskell's authorial stance — comic generosity vs structural critique — which cuts across everything in this segment

questions.question: Daniel, you've argued that Peter's naval service isn't heroism — it's extraction of penance, a system converting shame into social worth. But Edmund, you think the opposite: the shawl becomes honourable *through* the act of grieving well. So here's the question for Daniel: if you're right that this is all machinery, why does Gaskell make us *feel* it so hard? Why does that burial scene land? Is she sentimental in spite of herself, or is sentiment itself part of what she's anatomising?
questions.intent: Push Daniel on the tension between his structural reading and the novel's emotional power — invites Edmund to defend sentiment and Oliver to talk about how the novel performs that tension rather than resolving it

questions.question: Oliver, you said the ghost in this novel isn't Peter — it's the space where he *was*. That's a beautiful way to put it. But I want to test it. When Peter actually comes back — when the ghost becomes a person again — does the novel know what to do with him? Or does his return feel slightly awkward, like Gaskell built a whole architecture around an absence and then had to answer the door?
questions.intent: End the segment on an open, slightly mischievous question about whether the novel's structure survives Peter's return — lets all three experts weigh in and opens onto themes of resolution, disappointment, and authorial honesty

steering_notes: This segment has genuine three-way friction: Daniel reads through class and power, Edmund reads through moral character and individual love, Oliver reads through structure and performance. The best moments will come when all three are forced to account for the same passage — especially the burial shawl (c7:p72) and Peter's letter (c7:p60). Don't let Edmund and Daniel fight for too long without pulling Oliver in on the craft question: how does Gaskell make any of this *work* on the page? Keep energy informal — these are three people who genuinely disagree and find that interesting. If Daniel starts lecturing, redirect to a specific word or phrase. If Edmund gets too abstract about virtue, ask him what it looks like in the sentence.
cross_engagement_targets: Daniel's 'redemption for whom?' challenge directly targets Edmund's burial-shawl reading — both quote c7:p72 but interpret it almost as opposites; this is the segment's richest collision point

Oliver's 'Gaskell is delighted' reading of the Lady Glenmire passage (c9:p99) contradicts Daniel's 'class anxiety audit' reading of the same sentence — get them both holding that passage at the same time

Edmund's insistence that the farmer's boldness (c14:p27) is simply good character, not political, runs directly against Daniel's reading of social codes as power machinery — Oliver's adverb close-reading ('boldly') can bridge or sharpen that disagreement

Oliver's structural claim that Peter's absence is more interesting than his return is implicitly challenged by Edmund's reading of the return as moral resolution — worth surfacing directly near the end

segment_name: Laughter as Survival: Humor and Social Endurance

questions.question: Oliver, you said in our chat that the Carlo passage is almost a performer's sentence — that the pause before 'insult were added to injury' is actually written into the prose. Can you read it for us and show us what you mean? Because I want everyone to hear it before we tear into it.
questions.intent: Get the passage read aloud to anchor the whole segment, and establish Trevelyan's reading of the rhythm and timing as a baseline the others can then challenge

questions.question: Daniel, you heard that. Oliver's saying these ladies are taking themselves seriously, that the silence is a kind of power. But your reading is almost the opposite — you said this is the book's cruelest joke. That their only response to humiliation is silent agreement, which changes nothing. So who's right? Is that silence power or is it the sound of people with nowhere to go?
questions.intent: Force the central disagreement between Rosen and Trevelyan into the open — agency versus powerlessness — and get Rosen to make his most provocative case

questions.question: Edmund, I know you want to resist both of those readings a bit. You told me you think this isn't really about class or power at all — it's about individuals practising goodness in confined circumstances. Can you make that case? Because it feels like you're saying Gaskell isn't writing social satire, she's writing moral portraits. That's a big claim.
questions.intent: Draw out Leigh's contrarian moral-psychology reading and set it up against both Rosen's structural critique and Trevelyan's solidarity reading, creating a three-way tension

questions.question: Daniel, let's go to the ending — the ladies clubbing together to keep Miss Matty in her house. You called it 'investors in their own containment.' Edmund's probably going to call it Christian charity. Oliver might call it solidarity. You're saying it's all three, and that's precisely the problem — the system has made those things indistinguishable. Walk us through the actual passage and show us what you mean.
questions.intent: Get Rosen to quote the c15 passage and make his most radical structural argument, which should provoke strong pushback from Leigh in particular

questions.question: Last one — Oliver, you mentioned the 'D—n Dr Johnson' passage, and you said the dash is doing all the work. But I wonder if there's something else going on there: the rumour, the 'I won't vouch for the fact,' the immediate need for everyone to make peace. Is that still warm comedy to you, or is Daniel getting in your head — because that sounds a lot like a community policing itself through whisper?
questions.intent: Use the sotto voce passage to test whether Trevelyan's warmth reading can survive Rosen's power-through-gossip reading, and see if Leigh's moral restraint argument can bridge the two

steering_notes: The segment has a natural arc: start by getting the Carlo passage read aloud so everyone's working from the same text, then move through the central agency-versus-powerlessness argument, then test both readings against the ending. The big risk is that Leigh and Trevelyan agree too quickly — both resist social-critique readings — so make sure Rosen gets real room to make his structural case before the others gang up. The 'D—n Dr Johnson' question at the end is a good landing point because all three have something to say about it and it doesn't resolve cleanly into anyone's thesis.
cross_engagement_targets: Rosen's 'cruelest joke' reading of the Carlo silence directly contradicts Trevelyan's 'act of psychological self-preservation' reading — push both to address the same sentence

Leigh's claim that the c15 arrangement is 'pure Christian charity' is almost word-for-word what Rosen's 'investors in their own containment' argument is designed to dismantle — get them talking to each other, not just to the host

Trevelyan and Leigh both resist the social-critique reading but for different reasons: Trevelyan says the humour is warm and affirming, Leigh says it's moral not political — these are actually in tension with each other and worth surfacing

Rosen's point that the novel's warm tone 'is part of the mechanism' is a direct challenge to Trevelyan's reading of Gaskell's genius — Trevelyan should be asked to respond to the idea that what he's praising as craft might be ideological cover

segment_name: Closing: The Small Rebellions of Cranford

questions.question: Oliver, you called the bread-jelly receipt the key to the whole book — which is a big claim for a recipe. Make the case. What is Gaskell actually doing when she has Mrs. Forrester take that thing to her grave rather than hand it over to Miss Pole?
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to open with his strongest, most quotable take on c12:p21 — the sovereignty reading — before the others can frame it their own way

questions.question: Daniel, I can hear you wanting to jump in there. Because you've been pretty clear that calling this a woman exercising sovereignty is almost too flattering to the situation — you'd say she's not free of the system at all, she's just running its logic into the afterlife. Is that fair?
questions.intent: Force Rosen to articulate the property-extended-into-death argument directly against Trevelyan's sovereignty reading — productive clash between 'refusal as power' and 'refusal as property logic'

questions.question: Edmund, you've been patient. Both Oliver and Daniel are treating these women as making a kind of political statement — one says it's sovereignty, the other says it's the logic of accumulation. You think they're both missing the point entirely, don't you?
questions.intent: Draw out Leigh's strongest counter — that these are acts of love and conscience, not ideology — and let him quote the 'only I would rather exchange my gold for the note, if you please' passage as the example of non-reasoned moral impulse

questions.question: Daniel, let's go to Miss Matty and the bank notes — c14:p53 — because this is where I think your reading is most provocative. You've said her gesture solves nothing, that she hands over her gold and feels morally cleaner while honest people still lose their savings. But isn't that a bit brutal? Gaskell clearly loves Miss Matty. Is she actually criticising her?
questions.intent: Push Rosen on whether Gaskell endorses or quietly indicts Matty's self-sacrifice — get him to commit to how conscious the novel's political awareness is, and create space for Leigh to defend Matty's inarticulate virtue

questions.question: Oliver, you flagged the 'From my dearest John' label — c6:p25 — and then said Gaskell just goes silent. Nobody else has really gone near that one yet. Why does that moment matter, and does it connect to anything these two have been arguing about?
questions.intent: End on the most emotionally resonant passage and let Trevelyan's modernist-white-space reading land — also tests whether Rosen's commodification frame or Leigh's moral-texture frame can account for pure grief and silence

steering_notes: The central tension to keep live is Leigh vs Rosen — moral virtue versus systemic critique — with Trevelyan as a productive middle voice who keeps pulling the conversation back to Gaskell's craft and her deliberate use of humor. Don't let the segment become purely academic: keep returning to the actual words on the page. The 'I can't explain myself' stutter is the passage all three experts find significant but for completely different reasons — that's the best cross-engagement moment in the segment. If energy drops, ask someone to read the passage aloud before commenting. Watch for Rosen overloading with theory; redirect him to the text. Leigh may get testy if he feels the political readings are crowding out his moral one — that friction is useful, don't smooth it over too quickly.
cross_engagement_targets: All three experts cite 'I can't explain myself' from c14:p53 but interpret the stutter completely differently — Leigh sees genuine moral impulse that exceeds language, Trevelyan sees integrity living in the gap between feeling and speech, Rosen sees the inadequacy of available moral language to name financial violence. Put these readings directly against each other.

Trevelyan's 'sovereignty' reading of the bread-jelly bequest (c12:p21) and Rosen's 'property logic extended into death' reading are direct contradictions using the same textual evidence — force them to address each other's framing explicitly rather than talk past it.

Leigh's pre-interview note that Trevelyan will read these as feminist resistance, and Trevelyan's pre-interview note that he'd push back if Edmund argued the women were powerless — they've already anticipated each other's arguments, which means there's a real disagreement waiting to surface. Find the moment to let it.
